externalReferences.title: Feedback on Horror Map

inspection.evidence: Reviewed the first post and 1 representative image from the source page; only observations and the source URL are retained.

observations.text: A raised central island inside a circular perimeter creates one dominant landmark, a readable loop, and controlled approach angles.
Large blocky walls, sparse trees, and broad platforms remain legible from the overhead view without relying on detailed textures.
Hazards placed along the lower ring shape movement around the center instead of scattering danger evenly across the whole map.
The bright neutral presentation demonstrates that clear geometry alone does not create horror; mood needs deliberate local contrast and occlusion.

cautions: Use this source for spatial readability and low-poly massing, not as the target lighting treatment.

externalReferences.title: Chenami : User Interface Portfolio (UI/UX)
externalReferences.sourceScope: Resort Life, RoVille, LankyBox Simulator, Anime Universe, Anime Simulator, Anime Quest, and related shop sections

inspection.evidence: Reviewed the first post and 16 representative images from the source page; only observations and the source URL are retained.

observations.text: Resort Life and RoVille split customization, inventory, pets, vehicles, homes, and marketplace content into focused panels with a persistent side rail.
RoVille marketplace cards pair a scene thumbnail with category and ownership information while keeping the world visible behind the modal.
Small always-available social and build controls sit at the edges, while large task panels appear only when needed.
Simulator pet and trade screens use uniform card grids, a selected-item pane, and explicit offer state instead of packing all data into each tile.
LankyBox Simulator uses large paper-like cards and clear currency counters to make purchasing readable against a colorful world.
Anime interfaces keep health and currency persistent while character, quest, achievement, and reward panels occupy a centered modal layer.
Character and skill collections use portrait cards, rarity or role accents, and a separate detail or action region.
Anime Universe and Anime Quest separate buy, upgrade, and reward states through different panel structures instead of recoloring one generic popup.
Selected, locked, ready, claimed, and request states are communicated with both labels and color, reducing reliance on color alone.

cautions: The page spans several projects and years; reuse the information architecture and state patterns, not any one project skin.

licence.note: The page was reviewed as visual research. No reusable asset, media, or code licence was verified; do not copy source media or implementation.

implementationLinks.rationale: Horror still needs health, stamina, light, or objective state, but the HUD must preserve the threat area and survive small screens.
rules: Keep survival meters on device-safe edges and verify them with Studio Device Emulator so notches and Roblox controls do not cover critical state.
Animate the fill or color of a compact meter instead of opening a large warning panel that blocks the player view during danger.

implementationLinks.rationale: The official contextual-purchase guidance distinguishes pre-play and in-play moments, which is essential when a purchase could break tension.
rules: Place consumables or run upgrades in a lobby or pre-run shop before the chase begins, where the player can compare choices without losing control.
Allow enough uninterrupted time for the full purchase flow; do not trigger an offer while the player must flee, hide, or complete a timed interaction.

implementationLinks.rationale: Flashlights, keys, cameras, and defensive items map naturally to Roblox Tool behavior and inventory metadata.
rules: Give each usable item a clear TextureId and ToolTip so the hotbar communicates function even when the environment is dark.
Weld multi-part physical tools into one unit and keep equipped parts unanchored so a flashlight or key cannot pin the character in place.

implementationLinks.rationale: Greyboxing exposes traversal, scale, sightline, and vantage defects before horror atmosphere makes them harder to diagnose.
rules: Block the pursuit loop, hiding spaces, dead ends, and return routes with simple shapes before building detailed rooms.
Playtest every long sightline and elevated position so the monster cannot see or reach the player through an unintended unfair angle.

implementationLinks.rationale: MeshParts support strong silhouettes and reusable props while still requiring deliberate collision and scale choices.
rules: Design doors, cabinets, lamps, and creature-adjacent props around one readable silhouette before adding surface detail.
Choose collision behavior that follows the playable outline; invisible snags around dark props are read as broken movement, not tension.

implementationLinks.rationale: SurfaceAppearance separates color, normal, roughness, metalness, and emissive response, allowing controlled material contrast without changing geometry.
rules: Use roughness and value differences to separate damp floor, worn wood, painted metal, and interactable objects under low light.
Reserve emissive or very smooth surfaces for cues such as exit signs, powered devices, or wet traces instead of coating every prop with equal shine.

implementationLinks.rationale: The official flickering-light workflow provides a bounded brightness sequence and loop duration that can support environmental storytelling.
rules: Give each flickering source an authored brightness sequence and loop duration rather than randomizing every frame.
Use flicker on selected route or danger cues and offset nearby loops so a whole room does not pulse in mechanical synchrony.

implementationLinks.rationale: ProximityPrompt exposes action text, object text, input bindings, hold duration, and exclusivity for world interactions.
rules: Name both the action and object, such as “Unlock” and “Basement Door,” so the prompt remains understandable when the prop is partly obscured.
Use hold duration for consequential actions and prompt exclusivity to stop several nearby doors or pickups from displaying at once.

implementationLinks.rationale: Obby controls and checkpoint state must stay readable across touch, gamepad, keyboard, orientation, and changing screen size.
rules: Use responsive layout and dynamic sizing so stage, timer, and checkpoint controls do not crowd the landing area on a phone.
Change input hints with the active device and keep touch targets large enough to hit while the player is moving.

implementationLinks.rationale: Checkpoint and intermission moments are safer purchase contexts than an active jump sequence.
rules: Offer skips, checkpoints, or temporary boosts after a failure or at a checkpoint, when the player has stopped moving.
Keep purchase timing outside precision jumps and leave enough time for the complete Roblox purchase flow before restarting the attempt.

implementationLinks.rationale: Temporary movement powers and route tools can use the standard Tool inventory contract.
rules: Give grapples, coils, or checkpoint tools distinct icons and tooltips so players can select them without testing each slot.
Keep physical tool parts welded and unanchored, and test the equipped silhouette so it does not hide the next landing.

implementationLinks.rationale: A playable-area greybox lets the team measure jump spacing, character scale, route order, and recovery before art polish.
rules: Test every jump with the intended movement settings and camera distance before decorating platforms.
Use placeholder color or material groups to mark safe route, damage surface, checkpoint, and out-of-bounds space during playtests.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roblox Parts provide a small set of primitive forms that are well suited to readable obstacle construction.
rules: Build obstacle families from a consistent unit size so widths, gaps, and landing depths can be compared and tuned.
Anchor static obstacle parts and keep decorative additions outside the collision silhouette of the intended landing surface.

implementationLinks.rationale: Material and color can communicate route function without relying on high-resolution textures.
rules: Assign clearly separated material or color families to safe surfaces, hazards, moving platforms, and checkpoints.
Check the route in motion and at distance; a decorative variant is unsuitable if it weakens the edge of a landing or hazard.

implementationLinks.rationale: Outdoor lighting guidance covers global light, local sources, atmosphere, and reflections while preserving a readable environment.
rules: Choose sun angle and ambient values that keep platform tops and edges separated from the background throughout the route.
Use local lights or emissive accents on checkpoints and goals, while keeping bloom and glare low enough to preserve landing precision.

implementationLinks.rationale: The Input Action System supports cross-platform actions and separate contexts for gameplay and menu navigation.
rules: Bind jump, dash, restart, and checkpoint actions across touch, keyboard, and gamepad through named actions instead of device-specific branches.
Disable movement actions while stage selection or settings are open by switching from the play context to a navigation context.

implementationLinks.rationale: Uniform grids and tables suit purchase buttons, production lists, resource rows, and upgrade catalogs.
rules: Use a uniform grid for build or upgrade cards so cost, output, and state occupy the same location on every tile.
Use a table layout for production rows where names, rates, storage, and actions must align for comparison.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roblox Shop organizes passes and eligible developer products into managed categories and supports Studio preview.
rules: Group tycoon offers by function, such as production, storage, speed, or cosmetics, rather than mixing every price tier in one page.
Preview the configured Shop in Studio and keep the in-world store naming consistent with the categories players see in the Roblox surface.

implementationLinks.rationale: A structured grid can present machines, workers, recipes, vehicles, or collected resources with stable sorting.
rules: Give every inventory tile the same footprint and move detailed production statistics into a selected-item pane.
Use LayoutOrder or an explicit sort so owned, available, and locked items do not rearrange unpredictably after each purchase.

implementationLinks.rationale: The environment curriculum builds a world from modular assets after composition and asset-library planning.
rules: Reserve the full footprint of future production lines and expansion plots during greybox instead of forcing them into leftover space.
Place one stable hub or landmark where players can reorient as the lot becomes denser with purchased structures.

implementationLinks.rationale: Modular environment assembly supports reusable wall, floor, roof, trim, and prop pieces that still form varied structures.
rules: Build machines and buildings from snap-compatible modules with shared pivots so each upgrade tier can replace or extend the previous form.
Create variation by combining modules, rotations, signs, and small props rather than making every tycoon purchase a new mesh family.

implementationLinks.rationale: Material and color families can encode production state, upgrade tier, and circulation without additional geometry.
rules: Use one base material family for the lot and stronger accents for active machines, purchase pads, and output destinations.
Keep upgrade tiers related through shared material roles; changing every color and surface at once makes progression look like a different game.

implementationLinks.rationale: Global lighting exposes ambient hue, outdoor ambient, brightness, exposure, shadow, and environment controls.
rules: Choose a global time and ambient palette that keeps purchase pads, conveyors, and resource drops readable across the whole lot.
Use shadow and brightness to separate active structures from empty expansion space without making unbuilt plots look broken or unfinished.

implementationLinks.rationale: World prompts can label purchase pads, machines, collectors, and upgrade stations across keyboard, gamepad, and touch.
rules: Use specific action and object text, such as “Upgrade” and “Ore Processor,” instead of a repeated generic “Buy” prompt.
Use a hold duration for expensive or irreversible purchases and prompt exclusivity where several machines sit close together.

implementationLinks.rationale: Simulator interfaces repeatedly present currencies, pets, boosts, worlds, quests, and rewards in comparable card sets.
rules: Use uniform grid cells for repeated collectibles and keep currency counters outside the scrolling collection region.
Limit each tile to identity and one or two high-value stats; move the full stat block and actions into a selected-item pane.

implementationLinks.rationale: Developer products fit repeatable purchases such as currency, boosts, potions, and consumable progression items.
rules: Use developer products for repeatable currency or boosts and separate them visually from permanent one-time entitlements.
Design product icons so the important silhouette survives the documented circular crop and group products into meaningful categories.

implementationLinks.rationale: The official grid layout is appropriate for pet, item, egg, boost, and world collections with stable cell sizing.
rules: Keep pet or item cards uniform and use explicit sorting for rarity, power, equipped state, or discovery order.
Reserve a separate region for equip, lock, delete, trade, and compare actions so each grid tile stays scannable.

implementationLinks.rationale: The world-construction curriculum supports assembling a coherent environment from planned modular assets.
rules: Place the core loop destinations around a visible spawn landmark, then use paths and elevation to fan out into later worlds.
Build each progression zone from a small reusable asset family and one unmistakable landmark rather than a dense field of unrelated props.

implementationLinks.rationale: MeshParts can provide stylized silhouettes for pets, portals, machines, trees, and rocks while retaining explicit collision decisions.
rules: Use a shared faceting and proportion language across portals, shops, resource nodes, and environmental props.
Simplify collision around decorative meshes so players do not snag on visual detail while moving repeatedly through the hub.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roblox materials and variants can separate progression zones and functional objects without requiring large texture sets.
rules: Give terrain, paths, buildings, portals, and collectible nodes distinct material roles that remain recognizable from a high camera.
Reserve the strongest saturation or emissive response for portals, rewards, and active machines instead of every decorative prop.

implementationLinks.rationale: Outdoor lighting guidance combines global light, atmosphere, local sources, and reflective response for a readable open hub.
rules: Use even global light for repeated navigation while giving portals and event spaces a controlled local-light identity.
Keep haze, glare, and bloom low enough that currency icons, destination labels, and pet silhouettes remain readable against the world.

implementationLinks.rationale: Prompts can expose portals, sell zones, machines, rewards, and shops with device-appropriate input labels.
rules: Name both action and destination, such as “Travel” and “Moon World,” so identical portal shapes do not create ambiguity.
Use exclusivity or distance tuning in dense hubs so the player sees one relevant machine or portal prompt at a time.

implementationLinks.rationale: Racing requires persistent speed, lap, position, damage, boost, or progress information around an unobstructed road view.
rules: Anchor telemetry to device-safe edges and test phone notches and built-in controls with Studio Device Emulator.
Use animated meter fills for boost, damage, or race progress while leaving the center and vanishing point clear for driving.

implementationLinks.rationale: Passes fit permanent access or privileges such as a vehicle class, garage capacity, or enduring customization entitlement.
rules: Present permanent vehicle or garage entitlements separately from repeatable currency so ownership remains understandable after purchase.
Reflect owned state in both the shop and garage, preventing a paid vehicle class from continuing to look locked.

implementationLinks.rationale: A uniform grid supports a garage of vehicles, liveries, parts, and tuning presets with comparable cards.
rules: Keep vehicle cards equal in size and use a stable order for owned, available, and locked entries.
Move performance graphs, tuning controls, and long descriptions into a selected-vehicle pane rather than shrinking them into every card.

implementationLinks.rationale: Greyboxing is the stage for measuring route width, sight distance, shortcuts, spawn safety, and scale before city dressing.
rules: Block the full racing line, corner radii, overtaking zones, barriers, and reset areas before adding buildings or scenery.
Playtest long straights and elevated shortcuts so one route does not create an unintended permanent advantage or impossible recovery.

implementationLinks.rationale: Vehicle, barrier, sign, lamp, and roadside MeshParts need readable silhouettes and predictable collision at speed.
rules: Simplify roadside prop silhouettes so direction signs, barriers, and hazards can be recognized before the car reaches them.
Use collision shapes that follow the intended road boundary; decorative overhangs should not catch vehicles unexpectedly.

implementationLinks.rationale: SurfaceAppearance can distinguish asphalt, painted lines, metal, glass, rubber, and wet surfaces through controlled maps.
rules: Keep road roughness and lane-marking value contrast stable across weather and time-of-day variations.
Use metalness and smoothness selectively on vehicles and guardrails so road and hazard edges remain the highest-clarity surfaces.

implementationLinks.rationale: The outdoor-lighting workflow combines sun position, atmosphere, local lights, and reflective materials for moving scenes.
rules: Balance headlights and streetlights with global exposure so lane markings remain visible beyond the nearest pool of light.
Use atmosphere and local color to distinguish districts without allowing glare or bloom to hide braking points and traffic.

implementationLinks.rationale: The official Input Action System explicitly supports acceleration, deceleration, boosters, and refuel actions across devices.
rules: Define named actions for steer, accelerate, brake, handbrake, boost, reset, and camera instead of branching by device in each vehicle script.
Switch between driving and navigation contexts so garage or pause controls cannot continue accelerating the car underneath the menu.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roleplay games combine chat, jobs, homes, vehicles, customization, and social controls across many input types and screen sizes.
rules: Use responsive layouts that collapse secondary social and customization panels before they cover the world on a small screen.
Change control hints for touch, gamepad, and keyboard while keeping labels legible and primary role state visible.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roblox Shop can organize passes and developer products into categories that match a broad roleplay economy.
rules: Group homes, vehicles, cosmetics, job perks, and currency into categories that mirror the in-world systems players already understand.
Preview listing and category changes in Studio and keep item names consistent between Shop, dealership, wardrobe, and housing interfaces.

implementationLinks.rationale: Uniform grid and table layouts support wardrobes, furniture catalogs, vehicles, jobs, and household storage.
rules: Use a grid for browsable items and a separate preview or details panel for color, placement, ownership, and action controls.
Keep categories and sorting stable across wardrobe, home, and vehicle inventories so each system does not invent a new navigation model.

implementationLinks.rationale: A roleplay city benefits from planned landmarks, modular districts, and a reusable asset library assembled into a coherent world.
rules: Give each district one long-range landmark and connect jobs, housing, shopping, and civic areas with routes players can explain to one another.
Measure travel time and social gathering space during greybox before filling streets with decorative buildings and props.

implementationLinks.rationale: Modular environment pieces allow many homes and storefronts to share construction rules without becoming identical.
rules: Build walls, windows, doors, roofs, counters, and trims on a shared snap grid with predictable pivots.
Vary storefronts and homes through signs, awnings, color roles, and small prop sets while preserving the same modular dimensions.

implementationLinks.rationale: Surface maps can distinguish close-up civic, home, vehicle, and retail materials while preserving shared geometry.
rules: Separate concrete, painted wall, wood, glass, road, and metal through broad roughness and value roles before adding small texture detail.
Use higher-detail surface treatment only on places players approach closely; distant city blocks should rely on silhouette and color grouping.

implementationLinks.rationale: Indoor lighting guidance balances global light, windows, local sources, shadows, atmosphere, and performance.
rules: Use window light and local fixtures to establish entrances, counters, seating, and exits inside public buildings.
Keep local-light ranges bounded so adjacent apartments or shops retain distinct moods and do not wash one another out.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roleplay worlds contain many nearby doors, jobs, vehicles, seats, shops, and home controls that benefit from named prompts.
rules: Use explicit action and object text such as “Start Shift — Café” or “Enter — Apartment 3B,” with localization enabled.
Tune distance, line-of-sight, hold duration, and exclusivity so dense interiors expose only the interaction the player is facing.

implementationLinks.rationale: Tower defense screens repeatedly compare maps, towers, upgrades, waves, and loadout cards in structured sets.
rules: Use uniform cells for tower and map cards so portrait, level, role, cost, lock state, and rarity occupy stable positions.
Set a maximum cell count and responsive size constraints so cards remain legible on phones instead of shrinking indefinitely.

implementationLinks.rationale: Repeatable currency, consumable boosts, and crate-like purchases fit developer products, while permanent privileges should remain visibly separate.
rules: Group repeatable currency or consumables by use and keep them separate from permanent tower slots or access entitlements.
Design product icons to survive the documented circular crop and use category names that match the loadout and tower collection UI.

implementationLinks.rationale: A tower collection or deck is a natural grid with a selected statistics region and stable sorting.
rules: Keep the collection grid focused on tower identity, role, rarity, and level; show range, damage, cooldown, and upgrade detail outside the card.
Use text or icon labels in addition to rarity color so tower roles remain understandable for players who cannot distinguish every hue.

implementationLinks.rationale: The environment greybox guidance is built around a three-lane combat map and explicitly tests vantage, traversal, material cues, and strategic space.
rules: Block enemy route, bends, build pads, objective, and camera views before decorating the biome.
Playtest whether every lane segment can be read and targeted from intended placement areas without one dominant or unreachable vantage point.

implementationLinks.rationale: Towers, enemies, barricades, and map props need distinct silhouettes and collision that does not hide or obstruct the route.
rules: Give each tower role a different major silhouette before adding weapon or costume detail.
Keep decorative collision outside placement and lane space, and use simpler collision for repeated rocks, trees, and fortifications.

implementationLinks.rationale: Material and color grouping can separate enemy path, buildable terrain, blocked terrain, objective, and biome decoration.
rules: Give the enemy route a stable material or value contrast that survives snow, desert, forest, and night variants.
Reserve strong material or color accents for build pads, selected towers, targets, and the base objective rather than all scenery.

implementationLinks.rationale: Outdoor lighting guidance supports biome mood while preserving route and tower visibility under global and local light.
rules: Keep the full enemy path and valid placement space visible under the chosen sun angle, atmosphere, and shadow settings.
Bound attack lights, bloom, and emissive effects to the event area so one tower cannot erase the lane or neighboring units in glare.

implementationLinks.rationale: Raycasting provides a world hit point and hit instance for cursor, touch, or camera-directed tower placement.
rules: Cast from the active pointer or camera into the world, then derive the placement preview from the returned position and surface.
Filter invalid geometry and show valid or invalid state before confirmation so a click never silently places a tower on the wrong surface.

implementationLinks.rationale: An FPS HUD must keep health, ammunition, objective, and ability state accessible without covering aim or target silhouettes.
rules: Keep health and ammunition in predictable edge zones and test safe regions with Studio Device Emulator.
Animate compact bars or counters for damage and objective progress while leaving the central reticle region unobstructed.

implementationLinks.rationale: Pre-play, lobby, and complementary purchase moments are safer than prompting a player during live combat.
rules: Place loadout, cosmetic, or round consumable offers before deployment or during a real intermission.
Allow the full purchase flow to complete without the round starting underneath it; never cover aiming or movement during a firefight.

implementationLinks.rationale: Roblox Tool behavior covers equippable weapons, tool icons, tooltips, physical handles, meshes, and welds.
rules: Give every weapon a distinct TextureId and ToolTip so hotbar and loadout identity remain consistent.
Weld weapon parts into one unanchored unit with a deliberate handle so equipping cannot lock or destabilize the character.

implementationLinks.rationale: The official greybox curriculum specifically demonstrates a three-lane team first-person map and tests playstyle, vantage, scale, and orientation.
rules: Greybox lanes, connectors, cover, vertical routes, spawn protection, and objective space before applying final assets.
Playtest long sightlines and elevated positions for unfair advantage, then use placeholder materials to help players orient between lanes.

implementationLinks.rationale: Cover, doors, crates, weapons, barriers, and machinery need readable silhouettes and collision that matches combat expectations.
rules: Design cover around crouch, standing, and vault silhouettes before adding surface detail.
Use simple predictable collision for repeated combat props so bullets and player movement do not catch on decorative geometry.

implementationLinks.rationale: SurfaceAppearance can separate concrete, painted cover, metal, glass, rubber, and emissive technology through controlled maps.
rules: Use value and roughness contrast to distinguish walkable floor, cover, doorway, and objective surfaces at combat distance.
Keep normal, metalness, and emissive detail subordinate to target silhouettes and route cues; material richness must not camouflage enemies.

implementationLinks.rationale: Indoor lighting guidance balances global light, local sources, reflections, shadows, atmosphere, and navigation.
rules: Use local lights to mark doors, objectives, stair entries, and cover transitions while preserving target contrast in adjacent shadows.
Test exposure and shadow settings from actual first-person sightlines so bright windows or dark corners do not create one-sided combat advantage.

implementationLinks.rationale: The Input Action System explicitly supports FPS battle and spectator contexts and cross-device actions.
rules: Define fire, aim, reload, crouch, sprint, interact, ability, and weapon-swap actions once across keyboard, gamepad, and touch.
Enable separate battle, spectator, loadout, and menu contexts so a binding cannot trigger incompatible actions in two states.

implementationLinks.rationale: Ability-heavy combat needs responsive bars, cooldowns, targets, currencies, and touch actions across changing device capability.
rules: Scale and reflow the ability bar, health, stamina, and target information so touch buttons never cover the combat center.
Swap visible input hints when the active device changes and keep every cooldown state readable through more than color alone.

implementationLinks.rationale: Repeatable currency, rolls, rerolls, boosts, and consumables fit developer products and benefit from clear category and icon treatment.
rules: Separate repeatable rolls or currency from permanent character access and label the result type before purchase.
Keep important character or item detail inside the documented circular icon-safe region and organize offers by the same categories used in inventory.

implementationLinks.rationale: Character, skill, weapon, trait, and cosmetic collections need uniform cards with a stable comparison structure.
rules: Use a consistent portrait-card grid and reserve a separate pane for level, rarity, abilities, equipped state, and actions.
Sort and filter by role or collection state so a growing roster does not force the player to scan one long undifferentiated wall.

implementationLinks.rationale: Arena scale, vertical routes, ability range, spawn reset, and camera clearance must be solved before stylized world dressing.
rules: Greybox dash distance, knockback space, aerial height, walls, and recovery routes using the final character controller.
Playtest whether large abilities can be read and escaped from each major area without the camera clipping into nearby geometry.

implementationLinks.rationale: Stylized rocks, trees, buildings, weapons, and arena markers can use MeshParts with strong silhouettes and simplified collision.
rules: Use exaggerated but simple silhouettes for dojo roofs, rocks, gates, weapons, and trees so the arena remains readable during effects.
Separate effect anchors and hit volumes from decorative mesh detail so combat logic does not inherit visual complexity.

implementationLinks.rationale: Material and color roles can support stylized worlds and gameplay telegraphs without detailed texture sets.
rules: Use broad flat material families for ground, structures, props, and hazards, with a limited accent set tied to abilities or teams.
Keep arena floor and wall values distinct from effects and character silhouettes so saturated attacks remain readable.

implementationLinks.rationale: Post-processing offers bloom, blur, color correction, depth of field, sun rays, and color grading at global or camera scope.
rules: Use color correction or restrained bloom to establish the world palette, while preserving neutral contrast around combat telegraphs.
Apply camera-only blur or grading for short states such as menus or special moves, then restore gameplay clarity immediately.

implementationLinks.rationale: The Input Action System explicitly names fighting-game abilities and move swapping as a use case.
rules: Define named light attack, heavy attack, block, dash, target, and ability-slot actions across touch, gamepad, and keyboard.
Use separate gameplay, character-selection, and menu contexts so a move input cannot activate while the player is editing a loadout.

implementationLinks.rationale: Survival depends on persistent health, stamina, hunger, temperature, durability, or objective state that must remain readable on every device.
rules: Place the most urgent meters on safe edges and verify phone notches, Roblox controls, and small-screen legibility with Device Emulator.
Animate fill and color changes for depletion while avoiding large alerts that cover nearby threats or resource nodes.

implementationLinks.rationale: Base, lobby, death, and pre-run moments are safer purchase contexts than active gathering or combat.
rules: Present optional supplies or run preparation at a base, lobby, or post-failure pause where the player is not under immediate threat.
Leave enough time for the complete purchase flow and do not resume weather, combat, or timed survival loss underneath the dialog.

implementationLinks.rationale: A uniform grid supports resources, food, tools, weapons, clothing, recipes, and storage while tables suit crafting requirements.
rules: Use a consistent item grid with clear quantity, durability, equipped, and locked states, and move long descriptions into a detail pane.
Use aligned recipe rows for ingredients, owned counts, output, and craft action so shortages can be scanned quickly.

implementationLinks.rationale: Large survival spaces benefit from planned landmark hierarchy, modular biomes, reusable assets, and tested routes.

implementationLinks.rationale: Atmosphere density, offset, haze, color, glare, and decay control distance, silhouette, weather mood, and time-of-day readability.
